stats.line: About 1 in 5 people who ever use cocaine are projected to become dependent at some point. Half of those got there within about 4 years.
stats.mirror: You only do lines on nights out and think you're safe.

basis.design: national survey, same people interviewed twice (NESARC)
basis.who: US adults who had ever used cocaine
basis.n: 2,259 adults who had ever used cocaine; 376 of them became dependent
basis.measured: estimated lifetime chance of going from first use to the older DSM-IV criteria for dependence

stats.caveat: A lifetime estimate from people's memory. It uses the strict older definition. The other 4 in 5 never reached it, but may still have had problems.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: The cumulative probability estimate of transition to dependence was 67.5% for nicotine users, 22.7% for alcohol users, 20.9% for cocaine users, and 8.9% for cannabis users.

stats.line: About 2 in 100 American adults used cocaine in the past year (2018–19). Among 18- to 25-year-olds it was about 5 in 100.
stats.mirror: You feel like cocaine is everywhere in your circle.

basis.design: national survey (NSDUH), every year 2006–2019
basis.who: US adults aged 18 and over
basis.n: 85,765 adults surveyed in 2018–2019
basis.measured: self-reported cocaine use in the past 12 months, and cocaine use disorder. Ages 18 to 25: 5.53%.

stats.caveat: Far fewer adults, 0.37%, met the criteria for cocaine use disorder. Self-reported. Your city or friend group can be very different.

ref.cite: Mustaquim D, Jones CM, Compton WM (2021). Trends and correlates of cocaine use among adults in the United States, 2006–2019. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: then increased to 2.14% in 2018–2019 … The prevalence among 18–25 year-olds in 2018–2019 (5.53%) was significantly higher

stats.line: 3 years later, about 18% of people who had used cocaine weekly had a cocaine problem, against 9% of those who used less than monthly.
stats.mirror: You use every weekend and think it can't hook you.

basis.design: national survey, same people re-interviewed 3 years later (NESARC)
basis.who: US adults who had used cocaine in the past year at the first interview
basis.n: 157 past-year users followed up: 40 weekly, 26 one to three times a month, 91 less than monthly (of 2,501 who had ever used)
basis.measured: How often people used cocaine in the past year, and whether they had a cocaine problem (DSM-IV abuse or dependence) at the second interview. One to three times a month: about 14%.

stats.caveat: Small groups: only 40 weekly users. After allowing for age and other factors, weekly use meant about 2× the odds. Some may already have had a problem at the start.

ref.cite: Aharonovich E, Scodes J, Wall MM, et al. (2021). The relationship of frequency of cocaine use to substance and psychiatric disorders in the U.S. general population. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: frequent cocaine users at Wave 1 (≥1x/week; 17.8%) … Users of cocaine <1x/month at Wave 1 (n=91) had the lowest prevalence of cocaine disorder at Wave 2 (9.2%)

stats.line: Getting hooked on cocaine peaks at age 23–25. Most who get hooked do so within 3 years of first use.
stats.mirror: You're in your twenties and using a bit more each year.

basis.design: national survey (National Comorbidity Survey), survival analysis
basis.who: US population aged 15–54
basis.n: 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; how many had used cocaine: unknown
basis.measured: age at first use, and age when people first met dependence criteria

stats.caveat: Older data. 'Most' means most of those who became dependent, not most users. Within 10 years, 15–16% of users had become dependent.

ref.cite: Wagner FA, Anthony JC (2002). From first drug use to drug dependence; developmental periods of risk for dependence upon marijuana, cocaine, and alcohol. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: Peak values for cocaine dependence were found at age 23-25. ... Most of the observed cases of cocaine dependence met criteria for dependence within three years after initial cocaine use.

stats.line: Of new cocaine users, about 5–6% were already hooked within 2 years of first use. Smoking crack or injecting made it more likely.
stats.mirror: You're a year or two into 'just partying' with coke.

basis.design: national household survey (NHSDA, now called NSDUH)
basis.who: US residents aged 12 and over
basis.n: 1,081 new users (of 114,241 surveyed)
basis.measured: share of recent first-time users who had met dependence criteria since they started

stats.caveat: Covers only the first 2 years; the risk keeps building after that. Self-reported. Young adults aged 21–25 had lower early risk here.

ref.cite: O'Brien MS, Anthony JC (2005). Risk of becoming cocaine dependent: epidemiological estimates for the United States, 2000–2001. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: Between 5 and 6% of these recent-onset users had become cocaine dependent since onset of use.

stats.line: 68% of men in cocaine rehab had had scary, short bursts of paranoia while using. It got worse and came faster over time.
stats.mirror: You check the window or the door after a few lines.

basis.design: interview study
basis.who: cocaine-dependent men entering a 28-day rehab program, one after another
basis.n: 50 men in rehab
basis.measured: whether they had had very distressing, short-lived paranoid states while using cocaine

stats.caveat: Small, older study of dependent men in rehab; lighter users likely have it less. The paranoia passed after use; it was not lasting illness.

ref.cite: Satel SL, Southwick SM, Gawin FH (1991). Clinical features of cocaine-induced paranoia. American Journal of Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Thirty-four (68%) of the 50 men reported highly distressing transient paranoid states in the context of cocaine use.

stats.line: In people off cocaine up to 12 weeks, 46 studies found moderately worse scores in 8 areas of thinking, including attention and memory.
stats.mirror: You forget things at work and act before you think.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 46 studies
basis.who: people with cocaine abuse or dependence vs. healthy comparison groups
basis.n: 46 studies; how many people took part: unknown
basis.measured: test scores in 11 areas of thinking, split by how long people had been off cocaine

stats.caveat: Group averages, not a prediction for you. The gaps were small in people off 20 weeks or more.

ref.cite: Potvin S, Stavro K, Rizkallah E, et al. (2014). Cocaine and cognition: a systematic quantitative review. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
ref.quote: Findings revealed moderate impairment across 8 cognitive domains during intermediate abstinence. The most impaired domains were attention, impulsivity, verbal learning/memory, and working memory.

stats.line: Of men treated for cocaine addiction in 1988–89, 52% had been cocaine-free for 5 years or more when checked 12 years later.
stats.mirror: You think cocaine addiction is a life sentence.

basis.design: cohort followed 12 years
basis.who: men (veterans) admitted to treatment for cocaine dependence in 1988–1989
basis.n: 266 men interviewed at 12 years
basis.measured: whether they had used no cocaine for at least 5 years at the 12-year interview

stats.caveat: Only men who were found and interviewed. All had been in treatment. It does not say how many attempts it took.

ref.cite: Herbeck DM, Hser YI, Lu AT, et al. (2006). A 12-year follow-up study of psychiatric symptomatology among cocaine-dependent men. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: Of the 266 study participants interviewed at the 12-year follow-up, 138 (52%) had been cocaine abstinent for 5 years or more.

stats.line: Felt craving was strongest 2 days after stopping and fell steadily up to 1 year. Only a brain-wave signal to cocaine pictures was higher at 1 and 6 months.
stats.mirror: You're a few weeks off coke and wonder if the pull ever fades.

basis.design: lab study comparing groups off cocaine for different lengths of time
basis.who: adults addicted to cocaine, off for 2 days, 1 week, 1 month, 6 months or 1 year
basis.n: 76 people in 5 groups: 19 off 2 days, 20 off 1 week, 15 off 1 month, 12 off 6 months, 10 off 1 year
basis.measured: self-rated craving, and 'wanting' after seeing cocaine pictures, plus a brain-wave (EEG) response to the same pictures

stats.caveat: Different people at each time point, not the same people followed. Small groups. Whether the brain signal leads to slips was not tested.

ref.cite: Parvaz MA, Moeller SJ, Goldstein RZ (2016). Incubation of cue-induced craving in adults addicted to cocaine measured by electroencephalography. JAMA Psychiatry.
ref.quote: the subjective assessment of baseline craving … and cue-induced liking … and wanting … of cocaine showed a linear decline from 2 days to 1 year of abstinence

stats.line: Two weeks off cocaine, people said they slept well, but sleep tests showed their sleep was at its worst.
stats.mirror: You're two weeks off coke and sure you're sleeping fine.

basis.design: 23-day inpatient lab study
basis.who: chronic cocaine users
basis.n: 12 long-term users in a lab
basis.measured: sleep by overnight brain-wave recording vs. their own ratings, plus alertness and learning

stats.caveat: Only 12 people in a lab. It shows sleep can feel better than it is. Alertness and learning also dipped then.

ref.cite: Morgan PT, Pace-Schott EF, Sahul ZH, et al. (2006). Sleep, sleep-dependent procedural learning and vigilance in chronic cocaine users: evidence for occult insomnia. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: total sleep time and sleep latency were at their worst by 14-17 days of abstinence while self-reported sleep was at its best.

stats.line: Users who cut cocaine by about 72% did a little better on thinking tests within a year. Those who stopped completely scored like non-users.
stats.mirror: You're worried cocaine left you permanently slower.

basis.design: cohort followed 1 year (Zurich Cocaine Cognition Study)
basis.who: cocaine users and people who never used stimulants
basis.n: 19 users who cut down (those who stopped were some of them), 19 who used more, 19 the same, and 48 non-users
basis.measured: 13 test scores (attention, working memory, memory, planning) at the start and after 1 year; use checked with hair tests

stats.caveat: Small groups of mostly moderate users. The study doesn't say exactly how many stopped. People who started young recovered working memory less well.

ref.cite: Vonmoos M, Hulka LM, Preller KH, et al. (2014). Cognitive impairment in cocaine users is drug-induced but partially reversible: evidence from a longitudinal study. Neuropsychopharmacology.
ref.quote: decreased cocaine use (-72%) was linked to small cognitive improvements in all four domains. Importantly, users who ceased taking cocaine seemed to recover completely

stats.line: Twelve years after treatment, men who stayed off cocaine had fewer mental-health symptoms than men still using, on 4 of 5 measures.
stats.mirror: You wonder if the anxiety and low mood will ever lift.

basis.design: cohort followed 12 years
basis.who: men (veterans) admitted to treatment for cocaine dependence in 1988–1989
basis.n: 138 men off cocaine 5+ years, compared with the rest (266 in all)
basis.measured: a 58-item checklist of mental-health symptoms at intake and at 1, 2 and 12 years

stats.caveat: Both groups improved in the first year. A link: men who stayed off may have differed from the start. Men only.

ref.cite: Herbeck DM, Hser YI, Lu AT, et al. (2006). A 12-year follow-up study of psychiatric symptomatology among cocaine-dependent men. Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: By 12-year follow-up, the abstinent group reported significantly lower SCL scores than the non-abstinent group on 4 of the 5 symptom measures.

stats.line: In men who stopped cocaine, low mood and craving were worst on the first day and eased steadily over 28 days.
stats.mirror: You're in your first days off coke and feel low.

basis.design: controlled residential study
basis.who: male cocaine addicts, mostly injecting, living in a research unit, vs. non-addicted men
basis.n: 12 users, 10 non-users for comparison
basis.where: USA (National Institute on Drug Abuse unit, Maryland)
basis.measured: mood, craving and sleep ratings over 28 days

stats.caveat: Tiny, old study of mostly injecting users, with no cocaine around. Their mood was still worse than the controls'.

ref.cite: Weddington WW, Brown BS, Haertzen CA, et al. (1990). Changes in mood, craving, and sleep during short-term abstinence reported by male cocaine addicts. Archives of General Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Addicts' mood-distress scores and craving for cocaine were greatest at admission and decreased gradually and steadily during the 28-day study.

stats.line: Thinking problems tend to stay through the first months off cocaine, then may fade after about 5 months clean.
stats.mirror: You're two or three months off coke and still feel foggy.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 46 studies
basis.who: people with cocaine abuse or dependence vs. healthy comparison groups
basis.n: 46 studies; how many people took part: unknown
basis.measured: test scores by time off: still testing positive, up to 12 weeks, 20 weeks or more

stats.caveat: 'May' is the authors' word: fewer studies looked at long abstinence. Group averages, not a promise for you.

ref.cite: Potvin S, Stavro K, Rizkallah E, et al. (2014). Cocaine and cognition: a systematic quantitative review. Journal of Addiction Medicine.
ref.quote: Cognitive dysfunctions remain stable during the first months of abstinence and may abate after 5 months of sobriety.

stats.line: Half of Americans who had ever been hooked on cocaine were free of every sign of it within about 5 years. By the time they were asked, 336 of 408 already were.
stats.mirror: You've been hooked a couple of years and can't see the way out.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled and modelled over a lifetime
basis.who: adults who had ever been dependent on cocaine
basis.n: 408 adults who had ever been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed); 336 of them had got free
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared, and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as people recalled it. Getting free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using. Alcohol took 14 years, nicotine 26. For cocaine, 8.6% got free within the first year and 75.8% within 10 years.

stats.caveat: The study projects that 99.2% get free at some point in life; that is a model, not a head count. People in prisons or hospitals weren't surveyed, so the real pace may be slower. Men got free more slowly than women.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
ref.quote: Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset, respectively.

stats.line: Of 430 crack smokers recruited in the community in one US city, 63.6% never had a 6-month break from crack while the study ran (1996–2005).
stats.mirror: You've used for years and have never managed six months off.

basis.design: community sample interviewed again and again from 1996 to 2005; no treatment needed to take part
basis.who: adults smoking crack, with a positive urine test at the start
basis.n: 430 people
basis.measured: Whether each person ever went 6 months in a row without crack during the study; a statistical model sorted people into 3 paths: no change, some change, big change.

stats.caveat: One city's crack smokers, found by targeted recruiting; not a sample of powder users at parties. The paths come from a statistical model, not a hand count. Men were less likely to get a long break. Breaks shorter than 6 months don't count here.

ref.cite: Falck RS, Wang J, Carlson RG (2007). Crack cocaine trajectories among users in a midwestern American city. Addiction.
ref.quote: For the majority of the people (63.6%), crack use was uninterrupted by extended periods of abstinence during the study.

stats.line: Of Americans who said they had got over a problem mainly with cocaine, 58.9% had used some help along the way: mutual-help meetings, treatment, medication or recovery services. The rest used none of these.
stats.mirror: You think quitting coke alone is impossible.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot
basis.who: adults who said they used to have a problem with alcohol or drugs but no longer do, and named cocaine or crack as the main one
basis.n: 2,002 adults who had got over a problem; cocaine was the main one for 10.0% of them (a weighted share; the head count isn't stated)
basis.measured: Ever used, at any point: mutual-help groups (such as NA or Cocaine Anonymous), treatment, medication or recovery services. Across all substances 54% used help; mutual-help groups were the most common (45%). For alcohol it was 56%, for weed 46%.

stats.caveat: Self-report. Help could be one meeting or years of treatment. It doesn't show which route worked better; people with worse problems used help more.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Bergman B, Hoeppner BB, Vilsaint C, White WL (2017). Prevalence and pathways of recovery from drug and alcohol problems in the United States population: implications for practice, research, and policy. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: Factors associated with choosing assisted (54%) vs. unassisted problem resolution. … Cocaine (e.g., coke, crack, freebase) 58.9

stats.line: Of Americans who beat a stimulant problem (cocaine, meth and the like), half needed 2 serious tries or fewer. A few needed many more.
stats.mirror: You've tried to quit coke before and it didn't stick.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot
basis.who: adults who said they used to have a problem with alcohol or drugs but no longer do, and named a stimulant as the main one
basis.n: The study doesn't say how many of the 2,002 had a stimulant as their main problem
basis.measured: Number of serious tries before the problem was resolved, as people remembered it, counting everyone, including people who never needed a serious try. The middle half needed 1 to 5; the average was about 4.6.

stats.caveat: Stimulants as a group, not cocaine alone. Counts only people who succeeded, from memory.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG, White WL, Hoeppner BB (2019). How many recovery attempts does it take to successfully resolve an alcohol or drug problem? Estimates and correlates from a national study of recovering U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
ref.quote: Mean (SD) Median (IQR) Min, max … Stimulants 4.64 (8.03) 2 (1, 5) 0, 100

stats.line: Rewards for clean urine tests plus the community reinforcement approach (help building a life without cocaine) gave about 3 times the odds of being clean at the longest follow-up, compared with usual care.
stats.mirror: You respond better to rewards and structure than to willpower talks.

basis.design: network meta-analysis of 50 randomised trials
basis.who: adults with cocaine and/or amphetamine addiction; all 8 trials of this combination were in cocaine users
basis.n: 8 trials tested this combination, with 19 to 50 people in that group each (6,942 people in all 50 trials)
basis.where: the 8 trials of this method: US and Spain
basis.measured: share clean on urine tests, compared with usual care, at the end of treatment, at 12 weeks and at the longest follow-up after treatment. The program ran 24 weeks in these trials.

stats.caveat: Odds, not chance. At the end of treatment it was 2.8×; at 12 weeks 7.6×, but that estimate is very unsure (2× to 28×). Few, small trials, and only 1 of the 8 tested it directly against usual care; the rest of the comparison is indirect.

ref.cite: De Crescenzo F, Ciabattini M, D'Alò GL, et al. (2018). Comparative efficacy and acceptability of psychosocial interventions for individuals with cocaine and amphetamine addiction: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. PLoS Medicine.
ref.quote: and also at 12 weeks (OR 7.60, 95% CI 2.03-28.37, P = 0.002) and at longest follow-up (OR 3.08, 95% CI 1.33-7.17, P = 0.008)

stats.line: In treatment trials, heavy users who got down to 1–4 days a month by the end of treatment did about as well up to a year later as those who stopped, on most measures. Stopping still meant less cocaine at 6 months and more clean urine tests.
stats.mirror: You want to cut way down on coke, not stop completely.

basis.design: pooled data from 7 randomised treatment trials
basis.who: adults in outpatient treatment for cocaine (some also on methadone) who used 5 or more days a month at the start; 63.6% men in the full pool
basis.n: At 6 months: 114 who cut down to 1–4 days and 63 who stopped (of 716 in the 7 trials)
basis.measured: Problems with cocaine, mental health, work, the law and other drugs, 6 and 12 months after treatment, by how far people had cut down by the end of treatment. Only 38.3% dropped at least one level (for example from 5+ days to 1–4); 61.7% stayed at the same level or went up.

stats.caveat: Nobody was assigned to cut down; people did it themselves. Days of use were self-reported. Only 4 of the 7 trials checked at 12 months.

ref.cite: Roos CR, Nich C, Mun CJ, Babuscio TA, Mendonca J, Miguel AQC, et al. (2019). Clinical validation of reduction in cocaine frequency level as an endpoint in clinical trials for cocaine use disorder. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: among individuals at the high frequency level at baseline, those who reduced to the low frequency level at EOT had similar outcomes at follow-up as those who reduced to abstinence

stats.line: No medicine is approved in the US for cocaine addiction. Antidepressants, tested in 38 trials, showed no effect on cocaine use.
stats.mirror: You've hoped there's a pill that takes the craving away.

basis.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 randomised trials and 7 earlier reviews
basis.who: adults with a cocaine problem
basis.n: 7 earlier reviews and 48 more trials, covering 66 drugs or combinations; the review gives no total head count
basis.measured: Stretches of 3+ weeks fully off cocaine, cocaine use, and staying in treatment, medicine against placebo. Bupropion, topiramate and stimulant medicines may help a little (about 1.4 to 2.6 times as many off), on weak evidence.

stats.caveat: It means no pill has proven itself yet, not that every pill is useless. Three may help a little, but the evidence is weak.

ref.cite: Chan B, Kondo K, Freeman M, Ayers C, Montgomery J, Kansagara D (2019). Pharmacotherapy for cocaine use disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of General Internal Medicine.
ref.quote: Antidepressants were the most widely studied drug class (38 RCTs) but appear to have no effect on cocaine use or treatment retention.

stats.line: A computer program teaching coping skills, used weekly for 8 weeks, doubled the share who got 3+ weeks fully off cocaine: 36% against 17%.
stats.mirror: You'd rather learn skills on a screen than sit in a group.

basis.design: randomised trial
basis.who: adults hooked on cocaine who were also in methadone treatment for opioids; 60% women
basis.n: 101 people
basis.measured: 3 or more weeks in a row off cocaine during the 8 weeks: the program (7 lessons) plus usual care against usual care alone. Over the 6 months after, the program group kept cutting back more.

stats.caveat: One small trial, mostly women, all also treated for opioid addiction: a weak fit for most men who use cocaine. Clean urine tests and self-reported days off did not differ clearly. Lessons on a computer, not a phone app.

ref.cite: Carroll KM, Kiluk BD, Nich C, Gordon MA, Portnoy GA, Marino DR, Ball SA (2014). Computer-assisted delivery of cognitive-behavioral therapy: efficacy and durability of CBT4CBT among cocaine-dependent individuals maintained on methadone. American Journal of Psychiatry.
ref.quote: Participants assigned to the CBT4CBT condition were significantly more likely to attain three or more consecutive weeks of abstinence from cocaine (36 versus 17%, p<.05, OR=.36).

stats.line: Adding counselling or a reward program made people about twice as likely to be continuously clean at the end of treatment.
stats.mirror: You're deciding whether to get help or go it alone.

basis.design: Cochrane review of 52 randomised trials
basis.who: adults misusing cocaine or amphetamines
basis.n: 1,241 people in 8 trials (of 52 trials in the review)
basis.measured: continuous abstinence at the end of treatment, compared with no added treatment

stats.caveat: Low-quality evidence. At the longest follow-up the gain was no longer clear. Compared directly with usual care (2 trials), there was no clear gain. Many comparison groups still got some care.

ref.cite: Minozzi S, Saulle R, De Crescenzo F, Amato L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for psychostimulant misuse. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: increased continuous abstinence at the end of treatment (RR: 2.14, 95% CI 1.27 to -3.59, 8 studies, 1241 participants, low quality evidence)

rejected.claim: 18–25× higher risk of sudden death when cocaine is mixed with alcohol (cocaethylene; van Amsterdam 2024).
rejected.why: A death statistic. The owner does not want those, so it was not given a basis.

rejected.claim: European cocaine use, price per gram, and years from first use to first treatment (EUDA European Drug Report 2025).
rejected.why: EUDA's site returned 403 (Cloudflare) to every fetch, so nothing could be verified.

rejected.claim: 25 million people used cocaine worldwide in 2023 (UNODC World Drug Report 2025).
rejected.why: Only the UNODC press release could be fetched; the rules exclude press-release-only numbers.

rejected.claim: About 1 in 6 past-year cocaine users has cocaine use disorder (NSDUH).
rejected.why: No fetched source states this share. It could be worked out from 0.37% and 2.14% (Mustaquim 2021), but the rules forbid derived numbers. SAMHSA's own reports were blocked (403).

rejected.claim: Share who relapse in the first 1–3 months after cocaine treatment.
rejected.why: No fetched abstract gave a clear percentage (Sinha 2006 reports time to relapse, but no rates). Parvaz 2016 (how craving changes over the first year off) is used instead.

rejected.claim: How many quit attempts cocaine users usually make.
Cocaine remission about 14% per year, or 5% (Calabria 2010 review).
rejected.why: Only 4 cocaine studies, mixed definitions, and the abstract does not clearly say per year. Too unclear to show.

rejected.claim: Only 24.6% of Americans with a lifetime drug use disorder ever got treatment (Grant 2016, NESARC-III).
rejected.why: Verified, but covers all drugs, not cocaine alone. Left out.

rejected.claim: Money: what a regular user spends per year.
rejected.why: No official per-user spending figure found; price data (EUDA) was blocked. Not computed.
Only a 102-man mixed-drug clinic sample (32.3% had ED, Clemente 2017), not cocaine-specific. Not used.

rejected.claim: Prefrontal grey matter grew back after 6 months of no or less use (Parvaz 2017).
rejected.why: Verified, left out to stay at 14 new stats: only 19 people.

rejected.claim: Vietnam veterans: drug remission took 9 to 14 years on average and most last quit attempts used no treatment (Price 2001).
rejected.why: The summary mixes all drugs, and the full text could not be read (the publisher blocked the download).

rejected.claim: Most people addicted to illegal drugs quit by about 30, usually without professional help (Heyman 2013).
rejected.why: An essay that re-reads other surveys; its cocaine figures are not clear enough to show. NESARC (Lopez-Quintero 2011) used directly.

rejected.claim: 12-step-style drug counselling beat two kinds of psychotherapy for cocaine (Crits-Christoph 1999, 487 people); active 12-step work, not just attending, went with less use (Weiss 2005).
rejected.why: Verified (PMIDs 10359461, 15664719), but neither summary gives a plain number.

rejected.claim: Most recovered drug users had used treatment before getting free (Cunningham 2000, Ontario).
